story_text.value:
One of my favorite articles on Wikipedia is called "Timeline of the far future".[0]

The only problem with this article is the presentation: it's a gigantic wall-of-text table that does very little justice to the profound, awe-inspiring insights contained in it. This article deserves so much better!

So here's my attempt to dress it up a bit. Being a visual learner myself, and wanting an opportunity to improve my skills with three.js and typescript, I made a "reimagined" version of this article (with the help of some agentic assistance), giving it the visual treatment it needs so badly.

[0] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_the_far_future

story_text.value:
s3-accelerator is an s3-compatible nvme cache that serves hits in under a millisecond, replicates hot objects, and stays warm when the cluster resizes.

the hot object replication was inspired by groupcache [1], but that has some pretty nasty issues when the cluster resizes

s3-accelerator fixes that by: 1) using rendezvous hashing to reduce the remapping when the cluster loses a node, and 2) when new nodes are added, asking the old parent for a give key for the object rather than going to s3

It also uses learnings from cloudflare that it's better to cache on a second hit than a first hit[2]

It also uses ktls, splice, and sendfile so byte transfer of object chunks never hit userspace. That means it can hit millions of iops, or saturate 200Gb/s network cards, while sipping on CPU

it also is parquet-aware, and has an optional SQS integration to keep the cache fresh if an object is overwritten.

S3 stays the source of truth, and you can write through the cache (it wont cache the write by default)

these features make s3-accelerator uniquely performant, fresh, and s3 costs extremely low.

It's one of those "I'll build it one day" project ideas that Opus 5.5 finally made viable.

[1] https://github.com/golang/groupcache [2] https://blog.cloudflare.com/why-we-started-putting-unpopular...

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I'm co-creator of Television (https://television.run/).

Me and the team at Telepath (https://telepath.computer/) have been cooking on this and testing it with a few hundred alpha users. We just opened up the repo to the public today.

Television is a clean, beautiful place for all your artifacts. Think of it as a GUI for your agent harness, a visual space for creating and working with artifacts in collaboration with your agent. It works with any agent harness (Claude Code, Codex, Hermes, OpenClaw, Pi, OpenCode, etc) and uses whatever inference provider(s) your agent is already using. It's open source.

A CLI and lightweight server get installed wherever your agent harness is running (Linux or macOS for now). These talk to our macOS client app, which can be running anywhere (the browser is also supported with a few limitations). A set of skills tell your agent how to put artifacts on your TV's screen and modify them over time.

You use the client app as a sidecar -- i.e. you chat with your agent the way you normally do, but it can now respond by creating artifacts and putting them on your TV. Everything that ends up on your TV is yours and can be modified by talking to your agent. The entire UI, and your artifacts, are themeable.

We noticed lots of people are using artifacts in agents like Claude Code/Cowork and Codex, and lots of developers are spinning up little websites and webapps for working on projects, organizing their life or work, etc. But it all either ends up locked inside your agent's interface or as a mess of random tabs running on a bunch of ports you quickly lose track of.

We think that the future of personal computer interfaces isn't just chat, any more than it's MS-DOS. Artifacts are an early first step beyond chat. We think they should be easier to work with, and that you should own your own artifacts. So we made Television.

It's early but give it a try and let us know what you think: https://github.com/telepath-computer/television/

(BTW: we're building TV via an end-to-end fully spec-driven dev process, with custom tooling that also pulls in design and UI work. Planning to share more about that in the near future.)

title.value: Show HN: Television – an open source GUI for your agent harness

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I built Teacher Planner to help teachers organize lessons and prepare classroom materials in one place.

The digital planbook brings together lesson plans, units, schedules, and curriculum standards, with day, week, and month views, read-only sharing, and configurable print layouts. It supports English and Chinese, and you can try the planner as a guest without creating an account.

Alongside the planner, there are five AI tools: a lesson plan generator, worksheet generator, multiple-choice quiz generator, text rewriter, and writing feedback tool. These help produce drafts that teachers can review and adapt for their classes.

I'd appreciate feedback from teachers and people building education software. Which parts of your planning and material preparation still take the most time, and where do existing tools fall short?

story_text.value:
Portus is a Rust-based API/AI/MCP Gateway built on top of Rama as the networking stack (Rama replaced Pingora due to better throughput and lower resource usage).

Portus uses a split control/data plane architecture and conforms with the Kubernetes Gateway API specification (130/130 tests across all profiles).

Portus also runs in standalone mode outside of Kubernetes with a simple Yaml config file with ACME support built-in.

Please give it a try and if you like it then if you wouldn't mind going to Github and starring the project I would be very appreciative! If there is something missing that you would like to see then please leave feedback and I will see what I can do.

Thank you!

https://github.com/Portus-Gateway/Portus

story_text.value:
Hi there :-) New on HN, first time posting.

Past year, around December, I started experimenting with making ChatGPT and Claude generate source code in LDraw language.

This LDraw is literally an "assembly" language, a low-level programming language that describes how to assemble LEGO pieces together into models, one placement instruction at a time.

When executed by specific tools, like e.g. LDView, LeoCAD, Studio... these instructions become LEGO CAD models, that can be interacted with, modified, etc.

Or, in other words: one LDraw source file in .mpd or .ldr format is equivalent to one LEGO CAD model.

So, the idea I had was: if I manage for maybe ChatGPT or Claude to generate high-quality LDraw source files... then, they would actually be generating high-quality LEGO CAD models, right?

Then, after months of iterations and trying one thing after the other... it worked!!!

Long story short: using GPT-6 Astra and Opus 5.5, I've managed to create a python toolset, instructions, and docs for agents in general. Now, these can be used by them to generate LDraw models.

I've packed it all as a dockerized web app for others to try and experiment, with several providers (and agents) to choose from: OpenAI, Claude and OpenRouter.

Here's a bunch of exmaples: https://anteloc.github.io/index-samples.html.

If you are curious about the internals of an .mpd model, the "what was the agent picturing on its mind", open the .mpd file that got your attention on a text editor, and read the first line under the ones starting with "0 FILE".

I'd really appreciate feedback and comments, let's see where this goes =)

title.value: Show HN: Made an open-source Lego AI generator

story_text.value:
This is a full mechanization of the From Linearity to Borrowing paper in Lean https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3764117

The work was almost entirely done by Claude over the course of 3-4 weeks. It follows the paper and technical supplement as closely as I could and nearly every definition and lemma in the paper is covered, including the Fundamental Property and Adequacy (all well typed programs terminate with an empty heap, essentially).

The original paper is not mine and I have no connection with the authors, this was just a spare time project while I try and learn language design.

title.value: Show HN: A lean formalization of From Linearity to Borrowing

story_text.value:
I wanted a portable CPU implementation of kokoro for a project I am working on for a voice interface and found the current GGML/GGUF models were sometimes slower than python torch code. I love Kokoro for it's consistency and desired an easier way to integrate it into my projects. Focusing on a non-quantized SIMD yielded excellent performance for my targets. Theoretically portable to NEON and other accelerators though I have not tried. Hopefully useful for those of you looking for a less complex deployment of a TTS function that includes a G2P.

On the side I am exploring IPA more in depth and is where the g2p lexicon comes from. Espeak-ng involves tradeoffs on lexicon, emphasis, and frankly I just wanted to learn more about the subject. This kokoro work is largely in support of that exploration, but I figure it could be useful to somebody.

title.value: Show HN: Portable Kokoro TTS binary with g2p, normalizer, lexicon, and guesser
